flashcards.question: What is NAUTICAL TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
A special form of tourism in which the tourist's main motivation is travel and stay ON or BY THE WATER using vessels (boats, yachts, cruise ships) for leisure, sport and recreation.

It combines navigation/sailing with the use of nautical infrastructure (marinas, ports) and coastal/maritime attractions. It is especially important for Croatia and the wider Mediterranean.

(Note: this category is based on general SIT knowledge — verify against the professor's slides.)
flashcards.explanation: Tourism centred on the water and vessels.

flashcards.question: What are the main SEGMENTS of nautical tourism?
flashcards.answer:
• CRUISING — large cruise-ship holidays (mass scale; e.g. Mediterranean/Caribbean itineraries)
• YACHTING / SAILING — private or chartered yachts and sailboats
• BOATING / CHARTER — renting vessels (bareboat or skippered)
• NAUTICAL infrastructure services — marinas, berths, repair/maintenance

Nautical tourism therefore ranges from mass (cruising) to clearly special-interest (sailing/yachting).

flashcards.question: What is a MARINA, and why is it the backbone of nautical tourism?
flashcards.answer:
A MARINA is a specially built port for nautical tourism — offering berths (moorings) plus services: water, electricity, fuel, repair, supply, sanitation, reception and hospitality.

Marinas are the basic infrastructure that makes yachting/charter tourism possible. In Croatia, the largest chain of marinas is ACI (Adriatic Croatia International Club).
flashcards.explanation: Marinas provide berths + services; ACI is Croatia's main chain.

flashcards.question: Why is CROATIA a leading nautical destination?
flashcards.answer:
• A long, indented Adriatic coastline with ~1,200 islands, islets and reefs
• Clean sea, many sheltered bays and short distances between ports
• A dense network of MARINAS (e.g. the ACI chain)
• Favourable sailing climate (good wind, long season)

Nautical tourism is one of the highest-yield, more sustainable forms of Croatian tourism.
flashcards.explanation: Indented coast + islands + marinas = ideal for sailing.

flashcards.question: What are the main CHARACTERISTICS of nautical tourism?
flashcards.answer:
• HIGH per-capita spending (yacht owners/charterers)
• Strong dependence on natural conditions (sea, coast, weather)
• Requires significant INFRASTRUCTURE investment (marinas, ports)
• Seasonal but can extend the season (off-peak sailing)
• Sensitive to environmental impacts (marine pollution, anchoring damage)

quiz.question: Nautical tourism is centred primarily on:
options: Travel and stay on or by the water using vessels

quiz.question: Which is a segment of nautical tourism?
A marina provides:
Croatia's largest chain of marinas is:
A key reason Croatia suits nautical tourism is its:
options: Indented coastline with many islands and sheltered bays

learn.title: Nautical Tourism
learn.content:
⚠️ The nautical lecture slide is image-only (no extractable text). This category is built from standard SIT knowledge — verify against the professor's slides.

What is Nautical Tourism?

Tourism centred on travel and stay on or by the water using vessels — combining sailing/navigation with marina infrastructure and coastal attractions.

Segments

  • Cruising — large cruise-ship holidays (mass scale)
  • Yachting / sailing — private or chartered yachts (special interest)
  • Charter / boating — renting vessels (bareboat or skippered)
  • Marina services — berths + water, fuel, repair, hospitality

Croatia

Indented Adriatic coast, ~1,200 islands, dense ACI marina network, good sailing climate → one of the highest-yield, more sustainable forms of Croatian tourism.

flashcards.question: What is SPORTS TOURISM (UNWTO, 2019)?
flashcards.answer:
"A type of tourism activity which refers to the travel experience of the tourist who either OBSERVES as a spectator or actively PARTICIPATES in a sporting event, generally involving commercial and non-commercial activities of a competitive nature."

Sport and tourism have been linked since ancient Greece and Rome (competitions motivated travel).
flashcards.explanation: Watching OR taking part in sport away from home.

flashcards.question: Tourism vs sport: what is the core difference (de Villiers)?
flashcards.answer:
TOURISM is an EXPERIENCE-orientated activity (it provides people with experiences).

SPORT is a PERFORMANCE-orientated activity (competitive; rewards grow with the level of competition).

The famous 'coffee' example (Pine) illustrates the experience economy: a coffee can be a product (1¢), commodity, service, or — in a trendy café — an EXPERIENCE (500¢).

flashcards.question: What is the difference between SPORTS TOURISM and TOURISM SPORT (Gammon & Robinson, 2003)?
flashcards.answer:
SPORTS TOURISM — SPORT is the PRIME motivation to travel (the tourism element reinforces it).

TOURISM SPORT — the HOLIDAY/visit is the prime motivation, and sport is a SECONDARY activity.

Each has a HARD definition (active/passive participation in COMPETITIVE sport) and a SOFT definition (recreational participation, e.g. skiing/walking holidays, or incidental sport).
flashcards.explanation: Which comes first — the sport or the holiday?

flashcards.question: What are Gibson's 3 categories of sport tourism (2002)?
flashcards.answer:
1. ACTIVE sport tourism — travelling to PARTICIPATE in sport
2. EVENT sport tourism — travelling to WATCH/attend a sporting event
3. NOSTALGIA sport tourism — visiting sport heritage (halls of fame, famous stadia, museums) — linked to worship, heritage, pilgrimage and fanship

flashcards.question: What are Kurtzman's 5 SUPPLY-SIDE categories of sport tourism?
flashcards.answer:
1. ATTRACTIONS (stadiums, sport museums, halls of fame, sport theme parks)
2. RESORTS (sport as the primary focus, e.g. ski/golf resorts)
3. CRUISES (sport-focused cruises with pros on board)
4. TOURS (visiting multiple sport attractions/events)
5. EVENTS (sport events attracting spectator-tourists)

flashcards.question: How is DEMAND for tourism-sport classified (UNWTO, 7 groups)?
flashcards.answer:
By degree of involvement + importance of the tourism component:
1. Top-level athletes (the elite, <8% of athletes)
2. Second-level athletes
3. Youth groups
4. Sports enthusiasts & amateurs (the biggest group)
5. Tourists who want to practise sport when they travel
6. Tourists who practise sport casually
7. Spectators
flashcards.explanation: From elite athletes to casual spectators.

flashcards.question: How can MEGA EVENTS (Olympics, World Cup) benefit a host destination?
flashcards.answer:
• Re-brand / re-image a nation (Sydney 2000 accelerated awareness of Australia by ~10 years; Germany 'softened' its image with the 2006 FIFA World Cup)
• High media profile → world recognition; an agent of place-image change
• Long-term tourism boost after the event
• Benefits can be SPREAD beyond the host city (torch relay, training camps, cultural programmes, multiple venue cities)
flashcards.explanation: Mega events as nation-branding and 'fast-track' recognition.

quiz.question: In SPORTS TOURISM, the prime motivation to travel is:

Which is one of Kurtzman's 5 supply-side categories of sport tourism?

fillBlanks.sentence: In sports tourism, _______ is the prime motivation to travel.

learn.title: Sports Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Travel to observe (spectator) or actively participate in a sporting event (UNWTO, 2019). Tourism = experience-orientated; sport = performance-orientated.

Sports Tourism vs Tourism Sport (Gammon & Robinson)

Sports tourism: sport is the prime motivation

Tourism sport: the holiday is prime, sport is secondary

Each has a HARD (competitive) and SOFT (recreational/incidental) definition.

Gibson's 3 Categories

Active · Event · Nostalgia (sport heritage, halls of fame).

Kurtzman's 5 Supply-side Categories

Attractions · Resorts · Cruises · Tours · Events.

Demand (UNWTO, 7 groups)

Top-level athletes (<8%) · second-level · youth · enthusiasts/amateurs (biggest) · tourists who want to practise sport · casual · spectators.

Mega Events

Olympics/World Cup → nation re-branding (Sydney 2000, Germany 2006), world recognition, long-term tourism boost; spread benefits beyond the host city.

flashcards.question: What is LUXURY, and where does the word come from?
flashcards.answer:
Luxury is a MULTIFACETED concept — its definition depends on CONTEXT, GENERATION and NATIONALITY ('what one generation sees as a luxury, the next sees as a necessity').

The word derives from Latin 'LUX' / 'LUXURIA' = light, shine, excess, extravagance, deviation, lust.

Non-luxury and luxury are two extremes on a CONTINUUM — where ordinary ends and luxury begins is 'in the eyes of the beholder'.

flashcards.question: What are MASSTIGE and the 'democratisation' of luxury?
flashcards.answer:
MASSTIGE = 'MASS' + 'preSTIGE'. A luxury brand REDUCES its price to become affordable to the masses, without compromising quality too much.

This 'democratisation' of luxury makes luxury reachable to many consumers regardless of income — but risks harming the traditional narrative meaning of luxury (which is based on RARITY).
flashcards.explanation: Mass prestige = accessible luxury for the masses.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between INACCESSIBLE and ACCESSIBLE luxury (Chang et al., 2016)?
flashcards.answer:
INACCESSIBLE luxury — the extreme level of authenticity, prestige, exclusivity, quality and innovativeness; sought by the UPPER socio-economic class (the traditional understanding of luxury).

ACCESSIBLE luxury — non-essential, prestigious, authentic products that are publicly well-known and REASONABLY PRICED; consumed by middle/working classes to express social status.

flashcards.question: What are the 4 'lenses' for understanding luxury (Saviolo)?
flashcards.answer:
1. Luxury as a PRODUCT (durable investments vs personal goods; leather goods now dominate)
2. Luxury as a BUSINESS (4 elements: strong aspirational branding, superior quality + timelessness, high/premium pricing, aesthetics/design)
3. Luxury as a CULTURE (mainly European; France = 'art de vivre', heritage; Italy = excellence/innovation, 'la dolce vita')
4. Luxury as a CUSTOMER (heterogeneous; not all rich are luxury buyers; aspirational customers drive growth; Asia is booming)

flashcards.question: What is luxury NOT?
flashcards.answer:
• NOT just an object (it's objects + brands + business models + stories + service)
• NOT just expensive (it must give VALUE; high price signals quality but luxury ≠ expensive)
• NOT completely replicable (limited, made-to-measure, you wait — never a mass series)
• NOT easy (you need culture to understand it)
• NOT fast (true luxury needs TIME — unlike fashion)
flashcards.explanation: Defining luxury by what it is not.

flashcards.question: How do luxury SERVICES differ from luxury GOODS (Hemzo, 2023)?
flashcards.answer:
Luxury services share the general service characteristics — INTANGIBILITY, HETEROGENEITY, INSEPARABILITY, PERISHABILITY — plus:
• NON-OWNERSHIP (enjoyed for a limited time) but PSYCHOLOGICAL POSSESSION (valuable memories)
• LOWER conspicuous consumption (no visible logo)
• LOWER risk of counterfeiting (depend on savoir-faire/skills)

Managed with the 'service' 4 Ps: People, Processes, Panorama, Productivity.

flashcards.question: What is BLUXURY, and what is the scale of luxury travel?
flashcards.answer:
BLUXURY = combining BUSINESS travel with LUXURY leisure travel (cf. 'bleisure' = business + leisure).

The luxury travel market is projected to reach ~USD $2.7 billion by 2032. Luxury travel is SUBJECTIVE and increasingly about acute PERSONALISATION; the 'hierarchy of luxury travel needs' applies Maslow's pyramid to travel.

The first 'boutique/designer hotel' was Morgans (New York, 1980s).

options: Maximum prestige for the elite only
Mass prestige — luxury made affordable to the masses

quiz.question: Which is NOT one of the 4 'lenses' of luxury (Saviolo)?
According to the lecture, true luxury is:

fillBlanks.sentence: The word luxury comes from the Latin lux and _______.

learn.title: Luxury Tourism
learn.content:
What is Luxury?

Multifaceted, context/generation/nationality-dependent. From Latin lux/luxuria (light, excess). Non-luxury ↔ luxury = a continuum 'in the eyes of the beholder'.

Democratisation

Masstige (mass + prestige) makes luxury affordable to the masses, challenging luxury's traditional basis in rarity. Inaccessible (elite) vs accessible (reasonably priced) luxury.

4 Lenses (Saviolo)

Product · Business (branding, quality+timelessness, premium price, aesthetics) · Culture (France 'art de vivre' / Italy excellence) · Customer (heterogeneous; Asia booming)

Luxury is NOT

Not just an object · not just expensive · not replicable · not easy · not fast.

Luxury Travel

Services = experiences (intangible, non-owned, memory-based; 'service' 4 Ps: People, Processes, Panorama, Productivity). Bluxury = business + luxury. Market ~$2.7bn by 2032; first boutique hotel = Morgans, NYC.

flashcards.question: What is DARK TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
An UMBRELLA term for any form of tourism associated with DEATH, DISASTER and SUFFERING (Light, 2017).

The related niche term THANATOURISM (from Greek 'thanatos' = death) is more restrictive — it focuses on one's symbolic or actual encounter with death.

Examples: war memorials, holocaust museums, battlefields, concentration camps (many run by the public sector).
flashcards.explanation: Tourism linked to death, disaster and suffering.

flashcards.question: What is the central ETHICAL question of dark tourism?
flashcards.answer:
Where is the BOUNDARY between the ACCEPTABLE and UNACCEPTABLE transformation of suffering into a tourist attraction?

Dark tourism can be EDUCATIONAL and COMMEMORATIVE (ensuring suffering is not forgotten), but some visitors come for SENSATION / morbid curiosity / 'schadenfreude' — which can harm those emotionally affected. The right tone must be set, especially as many sites are publicly managed.

flashcards.question: What are some early HISTORICAL precursors of dark tourism?
flashcards.answer:
Dark tourism is not new:
• Roman GLADIATORIAL games
• Public EXECUTIONS (medieval to 19th century) — with grandstands for fee-paying spectators
• The alleged first guided tour in England (1838) — a railway excursion to see a hanging
• Victorian MORGUE tours and flogging galleries

flashcards.question: What is Stone's DARK TOURISM SPECTRUM (2006)?
flashcards.answer:
A 'spectrum of supply' from the LIGHTEST to the DARKEST forms of dark tourism, based on spatial, temporal, political and ideological factors that determine the perceived intensity of 'darkness'.

It identifies SEVEN dark 'suppliers' / products from light → dark.

flashcards.question: What are Stone's 7 dark tourism 'suppliers' (light → dark)?
flashcards.answer:
1. DARK FUN FACTORIES — entertainment focus (e.g. the Dungeons; haunted houses)
2. DARK EXHIBITIONS — education/commemoration (e.g. WWII museums)
3. DARK DUNGEONS — former prisons/courthouses (Alcatraz, Clink Prison)
4. DARK RESTING PLACES — cemeteries (Père Lachaise, New Orleans)
5. DARK SHRINES — places of remembrance near the death (e.g. Queen Elizabeth II tributes; George Floyd Square)
6. DARK CONFLICT SITES — wars/battlefields (Normandy D-Day, the Alamo)
7. DARK CAMPS OF GENOCIDE — the darkest end (Auschwitz-Birkenau)
flashcards.explanation: Fun factories → exhibitions → dungeons → resting places → shrines → conflict → genocide.

flashcards.question: Compare ALCATRAZ and ROBBEN ISLAND as dark dungeons.
flashcards.answer:
Both are island prisons that held famous inmates, but their tourist interpretation differs greatly:
• ALCATRAZ (USA) — associated with ENTERTAINMENT (the 'Hollywood' image, famous criminals & escape attempts); visitors may pose for fun photos in cells.
• ROBBEN ISLAND (South Africa) — more EDUCATIONAL and CONTEMPLATIVE; guides are former apartheid-era prisoners; visitors come to learn about Nelson Mandela and South Africa's history.

Lesson: how a site is INTERPRETED shapes the visitor experience.

learn.title: Dark Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Umbrella term for tourism linked to death, disaster and suffering (Light, 2017).
Thanatourism (Greek 'thanatos' = death) = the encounter with death.

The Ethical Tension

Where is the boundary between acceptable (education/commemoration) and unacceptable (sensationalism, voyeurism, schadenfreude) use of suffering? Most sites are publicly managed and need a careful, respectful tone.

Stone's Dark Tourism Spectrum (2006) — 7 suppliers (light → dark)

1. Dark fun factories → 2. Dark exhibitions → 3. Dark dungeons → 4. Dark resting places → 5. Dark shrines → 6. Dark conflict sites → 7. Dark camps of genocide

Interpretation Matters

Alcatraz = entertainment/'Hollywood' image vs Robben Island = educational/contemplative (Mandela). How a site is interpreted shapes the experience.

flashcards.question: What is HEALTH TOURISM (UNWTO, 2019)?
flashcards.answer:
Tourism which has as a PRIMARY MOTIVATION the contribution to PHYSICAL, MENTAL and/or SPIRITUAL health through MEDICAL and WELLNESS-based activities that increase individuals' capacity to satisfy their needs and function better.

Health tourism is the UMBRELLA TERM for two subtypes: WELLNESS tourism and MEDICAL tourism.
flashcards.explanation: Umbrella term = wellness tourism + medical tourism.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between WELLNESS and MEDICAL tourism?
flashcards.answer:
WELLNESS tourism — tourist is 'WELL' but wants to improve; PREVENTIVE, PROACTIVE, voluntary, lifestyle-enhancing (fitness, healthy eating, relaxation, pampering). More pleasurable/fun.

MEDICAL tourism — tourist is usually ILL; uses EVIDENCE-BASED medical resources; mainly CURATIVE (diagnosis, treatment, cure, prevention, rehabilitation).

Henderson: travel for WELLNESS (beauty spas) vs travel for ILLNESS (medical interventions).

flashcards.question: Who is the 'father' of WELLNESS, and how did he define it?
flashcards.answer:
Halbert DUNN (1961). He described wellness as NOT merely the absence of disease, illness and stress, but the PRESENCE of:
• Purpose in life
• Active involvement in satisfying work and play
• Joyful relationships
• A healthy body and living environment
• Happiness
flashcards.explanation: Dunn: wellness = the PRESENCE of positives, not just absence of illness.

flashcards.question: What are the 3 sub-sets of WELLNESS tourism (UNWTO & ETC, 2018)?
flashcards.answer:
1. HOLISTIC — a whole/global approach to healing (body, mind, emotion, spirit); complementary/alternative therapies, acupuncture, naturopathy (often at purpose-built 'retreat centres')
2. SPIRITUAL — broader than religion; seeking higher consciousness/meaning (yoga, meditation, Tai Chi)
3. MEDICAL WELLNESS

flashcards.question: How do cultural understandings of health/wellness DIFFER by region (Smith & Puczkó)?
flashcards.answer:
• CENTRAL/EASTERN Europe & Baltics — physical/medical therapeutic healing (medicinal waters, muds, caves)
• SOUTHERN Europe — seaside wellness, thalassotherapy, Mediterranean diet, relaxed pace
• SCANDINAVIA — outdoor recreation, sauna (integral to everyday wellness)
• GERMANY/AUSTRIA/SWITZERLAND — fitness + healthy eating + spiritual (yoga, meditation)
• ASIA — yoga, meditation, energy flows (Reiki, Shiatsu, Feng Shui) integrated into daily life
flashcards.explanation: Health/wellness mean different things in different cultures.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between MEDICAL TOURISM and MEDICAL TRAVEL?
flashcards.answer:
MEDICAL TOURISM — a trip for medical treatment where the patient ALSO uses the destination's TOURIST infrastructure (sightseeing, shopping, cultural activities); recreational prospects in (often exotic) locations.

MEDICAL TRAVEL — travelling for the SOLE purpose of treatment; the traveller may NOT visit tourist attractions. Many authors argue 'medical travel' is the better term, as patients can only tour if well enough.

flashcards.question: What FACTORS are shaping health tourism (UNWTO & ETC, 2018)?
flashcards.answer:
• More LEISURE TIME + disposable income for health/wellbeing
• Over-burdened HEALTH-CARE & insurance systems; rising long-term-care costs
• AGEING populations
• URBANISATION (over half the world lives in cities) → demand for escapism/natural alternatives
• LEGAL directives (e.g. EU Directive 2011/24 on cross-border health care)
• Global financial markets + investment; technology (m-health, wearables); data PRIVACY
• 'Reverse movement' of health travellers (developing → developed countries)
flashcards.explanation: Time/income, health-system strain, ageing, urbanisation, law, tech.

options: Ageing populations and over-burdened health systems

learn.title: Health Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Tourism whose primary motivation is physical, mental and/or spiritual health.
Umbrella term → WELLNESS tourism + MEDICAL tourism.

Wellness vs Medical

Wellness — tourist is 'well', wants to improve; preventive, proactive, fun

Medical — tourist is usually ill; evidence-based, curative

Dunn (1961): wellness = the presence of purpose, joy, health, happiness — not just absence of illness.

Wellness Sub-sets (UNWTO & ETC 2018)

Holistic · Spiritual · Medical wellness. Cultural understandings differ by region (CEE medicinal waters · Southern Europe thalassotherapy · Scandinavia sauna · Asia yoga/energy).

Medical Tourism vs Medical Travel

Tourism = treatment + use of tourist infrastructure; Travel = treatment only.

Factors Shaping It

Leisure time + income · strained health systems · ageing · urbanisation · EU cross-border directive · technology (m-health, wearables) · data privacy · 'reverse movement' of travellers.

flashcards.question: What is FILM TOURISM (Beeton, 2005)?
flashcards.answer:
Visitation to SITES where movies and TV programmes have been FILMED (and set), as well as tours to production studios, including film-related theme parks.

It is tourist activity induced by viewing a MOVING IMAGE — film, TV, pre-recorded products (DVD/Blu-Ray) and now digital media.
flashcards.explanation: Visiting filming locations, studios and film theme parks.

flashcards.question: What is the difference between FILM TOURISM and FILM-INDUCED TOURISM?
flashcards.answer:
FILM TOURISM — visitation to a site associated with filming; the INCIDENTAL experience of tourists at film locations (they may not have been motivated by the film).

FILM-INDUCED TOURISM — tourism that is INFLUENCED/MOTIVATED by film or TV; it specifically MOTIVATES people to travel to a film location.

(The Eiffel Tower is 'film tourism' by definition even for visitors who never saw the films shot there.)

flashcards.question: How are films 'PULL' factors in 'PUSH' locations?
flashcards.answer:
In tourist motivation theory, PULL factors attract the tourist to a destination, while PUSH factors predispose a person to travel.

Movies make destination attractions into PULL factors that are situated in the tourist-GENERATING ('push') location — i.e. the attraction is experienced VICARIOUSLY at home (cinema), with longer exposure than ads and no 'hard sell'.
flashcards.explanation: Films bring the destination's pull to the viewer's home.

flashcards.question: What are Macionis's 3 types of film tourist (2004)?
flashcards.answer:
By level of interest in film:
1. SPECIFIC film tourist — actively seeks out places seen in film (highest interest)
2. GENERAL film tourist — not specifically drawn to a location but joins film-tourism activities while there (moderate)
3. SERENDIPITOUS film tourist — just happens to be at a destination portrayed in a film (lowest)

(Connell & Meyer added the 'ELITE film tourist' — visiting purely to view the location, no other motive.)

flashcards.question: Are most film-site visitors SPECIAL INTEREST film tourists?
flashcards.answer:
NO — in short, NOT MANY. Most are casual/incidental/serendipitous.

Evidence: only 0.3% deemed Lord of the Rings the MAIN reason for visiting New Zealand (+9% one of several reasons); ~one-third of LOTR-tour participants had NEVER watched the film. Visitors are mostly drawn by the LANDSCAPE/scenery the film revealed, rather than the film itself (86% cited scenery for NZ).
flashcards.explanation: The scenery (not the film per se) usually drives the visit.

flashcards.question: What does the DUBROVNIK / GAME OF THRONES case show?
flashcards.answer:
HBO moved King's Landing filming to Dubrovnik (from Season 1, 2011); the Croatian DMO marketed Dubrovnik as a synonym for King's Landing.

Result (Tkalec et al., 2017): Game of Thrones film-induced tourism produced a ~37.9% increase in tourist arrivals, ~28.5% more overnight stays, and ~37.5% more City Walls tickets — far above the pre-GoT period. Depken et al.: ~59,000 additional overnights per year, with a STRONGER effect in the OFF-SEASON.

flashcards.question: What are the POSITIVE and NEGATIVE impacts of film tourism on a destination?
flashcards.answer:
POSITIVE: more tourists → more revenue & employment; infrastructure improvement; product diversification; cultural exchange; can fund HERITAGE preservation (admission fees).

NEGATIVE: conflict, COMMODITIZATION, loss of AUTHENTICITY, exploitation of natural/cultural environment; films can also project NEGATIVE images/stereotypes of a destination (e.g. drugs, crime). DMOs cannot control media representations.
flashcards.explanation: Revenue & heritage funding vs commoditization & stereotypes.

options: Sites where movies/TV have been filmed, studios and film theme parks

The _______ / Game of Thrones case is Croatia's famous film-induced success.

learn.title: Film Tourism
learn.content:
Definition

Visitation to filming sites, studios and film theme parks (Beeton, 2005) — tourist activity induced by a moving image (film, TV, digital).

Film vs Film-induced

Film tourism = incidental visitation to film sites

Film-induced tourism = travel specifically motivated by the film

Films = pull factors situated in push (home) locations.

Types of Film Tourist

Macionis: specific → general → serendipitous (+ Connell & Meyer's 'elite'). Most visitors are NOT special-interest film tourists — they're drawn by the scenery the film revealed.

Dubrovnik & Game of Thrones

King's Landing filmed in Dubrovnik (2011) → ~37.9% more arrivals, ~37.5% more City Walls tickets (Tkalec et al.); ~59,000 extra overnights/year, stronger in the OFF-season.

Impacts

+ revenue, jobs, infrastructure, heritage funding · − commoditization, loss of authenticity, negative stereotypes (DMOs can't control media).
